extracted.intended_audience: aspiring artists, poets, literary critics, and public speakers
extracted.subtask_description: Short prescriptive/critical guidance on making literature and oratory effective: where artists should draw inspiration, what makes poetry durable, and what distinguishes genuine oratory from mere elocution. Draws on examples (the Bible, Father Taylor, visitors to America) to illustrate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the school of heroic action as artistic training
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a still higher school for him who would kindle his fire with coal from the altar of the loftiest and purest art. It is the school of all grand actions and grand virtues, of heroism...of all the mighty deeds written in the pages of history--deeds of daring, and enthusiasm, devotion, and fortitude."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than only imitating the old masters' productions, the aspiring artist should study heroic deeds, martyrs, and great actions: these supply the deepest artistical impulse and material for sublime art. Examples given: Washington, Mary Stuart, Kossuth, Mazzini; the idea is to draw poetic fire from real moral grandeur and historic transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature must be rooted in the nationality's transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: "So long as such literature is no born branch and offshoot of the Nationality, rooted and grown from its roots, and fibred with its fibre, it can never answer any deep call or perennial need."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective national literature grows from lived experience, collective transactions, and the 'vivid, rapidest, most stupendous processes' of the country; polished or abstract works disconnected from the people's life will not achieve deep or lasting significance. The author criticizes relying on elite coteries (receptions, clubs) as a basis for understanding a nation's literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the 'transaction' before attempting record or poem
rubrics_metrics.description: "Before there can be recorded history or poem there must be the transaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry and recorded history presuppose real events, deeds, and collective life; the maker should engage with and depict actual social, moral, or historical action rather than inventing art divorced from substantive life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize psychological and religious depth over mere aesthetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding Oriental and Biblical poetry: "All the poems of Orientalism, with the Old and New Testaments at the centre, tend to deep and wide...psychological development--with little, or nothing at all, of the mere esthetic, the principal verse-requirement of our day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and emulate ancient models (Hebrew Bible, Hindu epics) for their spiritual, psychological, and thematic depth rather than their formal metrics; note that Hebrew poetry often lacked rhyme or strict metre—substance and spiritual impulse matter more than polished versification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bold, lawless metaphors and spiritual sensuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: On Biblical poetry: "The metaphors daring beyond account, the lawless soul, extravagant by our standards, the glow of love and friendship...unsurpass'd in proverbs, in religious ecstasy...the spirit everything, the ceremonies and forms of the churches nothing...faith limitless, its immense sensuousness immensely spiritual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should not shy from audacious metaphor or intense, sensuous spiritual language; such excesses can produce profundity and emotional power absent in cautious, overly refined modern styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create cumulative associations and universality in great poems
rubrics_metrics.description: "The culminated proof of the poetry of a country is the quality of its personnel...the finest blending of individuality with universality...Nowhere else the abnegation of self towering in such quaint sublimity; nowhere else the simplest human emotions conquering the gods of heaven, and fate itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeless poems accrue associations and responses across generations; aim for works that resonate with broad human experience and gather meaning over time rather than ephemeral cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory must be 'action, action, action' and convey live feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "The live feeling advanced upon you and seiz'd you with a power before unknown...the Demosthenean rule and requirement of 'action, action, action'...was the quality that had leading fulfilment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful speaker moves listeners through energetic inward and outward action: vividness, momentum, and authentic emotional force matter more than technical polish. The example of Father Taylor—no manuscript, powerful Biblical/allusive language, impassioned prayers—is used to illustrate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and unsophisticated practice often trump trained elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why is it that the unsophisticated practices often strike deeper than the train'd ones?...the first, last, and most important quality of all, in training for a 'finish'd speaker,' generally unsought...Though may-be it cannot be taught."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate genuine feeling, naturalness, and directness; avoid substituting ornamental elocution for authentic conviction. Technical elocution can be abundant, but it does not equal the moral and emotional grip of unschooled but heartfelt speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt imagery and references to the audience's life
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation of Father Taylor's pulpit and sermons: mural painting of stormy sea and repeated allusions 'to ships and the ocean and sailors' lives, of unrival'd power and life-likeness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, relevant images drawn from the audience's experience to increase rhetorical power; tailoring examples (ship imagery for sailors) enhances resonance and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor brevity, simplicity of argument, and minimal reliance on manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on Father Taylor: 'there was no sign of any MS., or reading from notes...A few arguments, and of the best, but always brief and simple.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches should avoid over-long, bookish displays; concise, straightforward arguments and spontaneous delivery often produce greater emotional impact than long, polished, manuscript-dependent addresses.
